bib.title: Personalizing Dialogue Agents: I have a dog, do you have pets too?

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Personalizing Dialogue Agents: I have a dog, do you have pets too? Saizheng Zhang, Emily Dinan, Jack Urbanek, Arthur Szlam, Douwe Kiela, Jason Weston (MILA / Facebook AI Research). ACL 2018 (Long Papers), proceedings pages 2204–2213.

COVERAGE: Read all 10 of 10 PDF pages (38,911 of 38,911 chars), references included. **This PDF is the 10-page ACL camera-ready and does not contain the appendices.** The text points to Appendix tables 5, 6 and 7–14, Appendix D (profile prediction) and an appendix with "more details" of the human-eval measures. None of them is in this file. Those results and the full wording of the human-eval questions could not be read, so they are left out below. Page mapping: proceedings p.2204 is PDF p.1, so p.2210 is PDF p.7 and p.2211 is PDF p.8.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: In human evaluation, ranking models beat generative models, and every PersonaChat-trained model beats Twitter and OpenSubtitles models on fluency, engagingness and consistency. Humans are the upper bound.
  number: Human 4.31/4.25/4.36, detection 0.95. KV Profile Memory 3.97/3.50/3.44, 0.81. Seq2Seq 3.17/3.18/2.98, 0.51. Profile Memory (gen) 3.08/3.13/3.14, 0.72. Twitter LM 3.21/1.75/1.95, 0.57. OpenSubtitles 2009 LM 2.25/2.12/1.96, 0.38.
  setup: A Turker chats with a model without knowing it is a model, using test-set personas. Scores are 1–5 (std in parentheses). 100 dialogues per model. The number of raters is not stated.
  quote: "KV Proﬁle Memory Self 3.97(0.94) 3.50(1.17) 3.44(1.30) 0.81(0.39)"; "Human Self 4.31(1.07) 4.25(1.06) 4.36(0.92) 0.95(0.22)"; "Twitter LM None 3.21(1.54) 1.75(1.04) 1.95(1.22) 0.57(0.50)"
  where: Table 4, p.2210 (PDF p.7)
- claim: The authors give the reason they used human evaluation and describe the protocol.
  number: 1–5 scale; 100 dialogues each
  setup: Fluency, engagingness and consistency are rated after the chat. Persona detection shows two profiles and asks which one belongs to the partner. Models: the best generative and ranking models, with No Persona and Self Persona variants.
  quote: "As automated metrics are notoriously poor for evaluating dialogue (Liu et al., 2016) we also perform human evaluation using crowdsourced workers." / "We ask them to evaluate ﬂuency, engagingness and consistency (scored between 1-5)." / "in both the No Persona and Self Persona categories, 100 dialogues each."
  where: Sec 5.2, p.2211 (PDF p.8)
- claim: Automatic and human metrics disagree. On hits@1, ranking models beat generative models by a wide margin, which the authors say may be partly because ranking is what those models optimise. Under human evaluation the gap is smaller and noisy, and adding a persona raises consistency but not engagingness. Example: KV Memory with no persona scores 3.88 on engagingness, higher than the 3.50 of KV Profile Memory.
  number: hits@1 0.511 (KV Profile Memory) vs 0.125 (generative Profile Memory), original persona
  setup: Table 3, 19 random distractors
  quote: "Ranking models are far better than generative models at ranking. This is perhaps obvious as that is the metric they are optimizing, but still the performance difference is quite stark." / "these differences are obscured by the high variance of the human raters' evaluations." / "models that have access to their own personas ... are scored as more consistent by annotators, although not more engaging."
  where: Sec 5.1 p.2209; Sec 5.2 p.2211; Sec 6 p.2211
- claim: The automatic metrics are perplexity, F1 and hits@1 (next-utterance classification, following Lowe et al. 2015). Table 3 reports only ppl and hits@1. The F1 numbers are not in this PDF.
  number: N=19 distractors
  quote: "(i) the log likelihood of the correct sequence, measured via perplexity, (ii) F1 score, and (iii) next utterance classiﬁcation loss, following Lowe et al. (2015). The latter consists of choosing N random distractor responses from other dialogues (in our setting,N=19) ... (called hits@1 in the experiments)."
  where: Sec 3.4, p.2208
- claim: Persona conditioning helps with original personas. Revised personas, which have no word overlap, wipe out most of that gain.
  number: hits@1 for Profile Memory (ranking): 0.318 none / 0.509 original / 0.354 revised. IR baseline: 0.214 / 0.410 / 0.207. Starspace: 0.318 / 0.491 / 0.322. Generative Profile Memory ppl: 38.08 / 34.54 / 38.21. Seq2Seq ppl gets worse with a persona: 38.08 / 40.53 / 40.65.
  setup: Table 3, test set, trained on original personas
  quote: "IR baseline - 0.214 - 0.410 - 0.207"; "Revised personas are much harder to use. We do however still see some gain for the Proﬁle Memory networks compared to none (0.354 vs. 0.318 hits@1)."
  where: Table 3 p.2210; Sec 5.1 p.2210
- claim: Why the personas were rewritten. Crowdworkers copy profile wording into the dialogue, so a model can score well by matching words. The authors cite SQuAD as a dataset with this problem. Revisers were told to write "a related characteristic that the same person may have", and the entry form warned them if they copied a non-stop word.
  number: none
  quote: "there is a danger that humans will, even if asked not to, unwittingly repeat proﬁle information either verbatim or with signiﬁcant word overlap. This may make any subsequent machine learning tasks less challenging, and the solutions will not generalize" / "if a non-stop word is copied we issue a warning, and ask them to rephrase"
  where: Sec 3.2, p.2206–2207
- claim: Training on the revised personas helps on both the original and revised test sets. The numbers are in Appendix Table 6, which is not in this PDF.
  number: none
  quote: "Training on revised personas helps, both for test examples that are in original form or revised form, likely due to the model be forced to learn more than simple word overlap"
  where: Sec 5.1, p.2210
- claim: Dataset scale and how it was collected. Mechanical Turk workers were paired at random, each given a different persona. Messages were capped at 15 words, dialogues ran a minimum of 6–8 turns, copying from the persona was blocked by string matching, and high-quality dialogues earned a bonus.
  number: 1155 personas (100 val, 100 test); 164,356 utterances over 10,981 dialogs; val 15,705 utt (968 dialogs); test 15,119 utt (1000 dialogs)
  quote: "This resulted in a dataset of 164,356 utterances over 10,981 dialogs, 15,705 utterances (968 dialogs) of which are set aside for validation, and 15,119 utterances (1000 dialogs) for test."
  where: Sec 3, p.2206
- claim: The collection instructions were changed after a pilot because workers talked too much about themselves. The authors say the instructions shape the metrics.
  number: none
  quote: "In an early study we noticed the crowdworkers tending to talk about themselves (their own persona) too much, so we also added the instructions "both ask questions and answer questions of your chat partner" which seemed to help." / "Certainly this is skewed by the particular instructions one could give to the crowdworkers."
  where: Sec 3.3 p.2207; Sec 5.1 p.2210
- claim: Profile prediction, reported here only in summary (details are in Appendix D, which is absent).
  number: 94.3% from a human's dialogue; 23% from the KV Profile Memory model's dialogue
  quote: "human speaker's proﬁles can be predicted from their dialogue with high accuracy (94.3%, similar to human performance in Table 4) or even from the model's dialogue (23% with KV Proﬁle Memory)"
  where: Sec 5.3, p.2211

LIMITS: The appendices are missing, so F1 results, the their/both-persona tables (5 and 6), the exact human-eval questions and the profile-prediction details could not be checked. The paper does not report rater counts, inter-annotator agreement or significance tests, and the authors concede the differences are "obscured by the high variance". Only 100 dialogues per model were collected. The authors concede the hits@1 advantage may come from the training objective, and that generative probabilities are "not calibrated well enough to give a sentence-based probability". The KV memory model was not trained directly: it reuses Profile Memory weights at test time. Conditioning on the partner's persona had little impact, which they attribute to the instructions. Dated: the models are pre-transformer (LSTM seq2seq, memory networks, GloVe).

BUILDS ON: Lowe et al. (2015) for hits@1 / next-utterance classification. Liu et al. (2016) for "automated metrics are notoriously poor". Li et al. (2016a) for persona embeddings. Sukhbaatar et al. (2015) for memory networks. Miller et al. (2016) for key-value memory networks. Wu et al. (2017) for Starspace. Sordoni et al. (2015) for the IR baseline. Vinyals and Le (2015) for the Twitter/OpenSubtitles baselines. Chen et al. (2017) for SQuAD word overlap. Voorhees et al. (1999) for tasks that are neither too easy nor too hard. Data and code are released in ParlAI.

CODE: None.

FIGURES: The figure script found no captioned figures. Table candidates:
- **Tables 3 and 4 on p.2210 (PDF p.7) are the best visual.**
  - Table 3: "Evaluation of dialog utterance prediction with various models in three settings: without conditioning on a persona, conditioned on the speakers given persona ("Original Persona"), or a revised persona that does not have word overlap."
  - Table 4: "Human Evaluation of various PERSONA-CHAT models, along with a comparison to human performance, and Twitter and OpenSubtitles based models (last 4 rows), standard deviation in parenthesis."

  Side by side, these two tables show at a glance how the automatic metric ranks models compared with human ratings, and how hits@1 falls when the personas are revised.
- Table 1 (p.2207, original vs revised personas) shows the word-overlap fix more quickly than prose.

PROBLEMS: Text extraction was clean, apart from the Table 3 header, which ran together into "Revised Personappl hits@1". There were no embedded instructions. Appendix content is absent from the PDF.
